[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, can you all hear me?
[00:07] Priya (Nimbus CTO): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Samir.
[00:10] Elena (Redwood SE): Morning — I'll drive the tech parts, Samir will cover the commercial bits at the end.
[00:15] Marcus (Nimbus): Great. We're mostly here to make sure our existing client scripts can be used with your harness and to understand how streaming behaves with our proxy.
[00:22] Samir: Perfect, that's exactly what we want to validate. Quick agenda: one — repo/adapter handshake; two — streaming vs non-streaming test plan and SLOs; three — data/telemetry + runbook; four — next steps. 
[00:38] Leah (Nimbus SRE): One thing up front: our proxy does mutual TLS and has a rate limiter that can do bursts but then holds back; not sure how that will interact with long-lived streams.
[00:50] Elena: Good flag. We can mimic that in the harness by adding a proxy layer in the runner, or run the harness behind your staging proxy. Either works but there are differences in measuring tail latency.
[01:05] Tom (DevOps): Our scripts use streaming chunked responses; we also have a fallback non-streaming mode for mobile clients.
[01:12] Samir: OK so we need both modes exercised. Usually we run a mixed workload: 70% streaming, 30% batch non-streaming to see interactions — but we can tune that to your expected production mix.
[01:25] Priya: Our expected mix is closer to 60/40 streaming to non-streaming. Also, important — our cost target per 1M tokens is a big part of the procurement evaluation.
[01:34] Samir: We'll include cost estimates in the runbook but the main focus of the pilot is correctness/latency and any functional incompatibilities. We can produce per-model per-quantization estimates as a follow-up.
[01:45] Elena: For the harness, two options: 1) run your client scripts unchanged and use our harness adapter (we provide a small shim library), or 2) wrap the traffic at the network level with a proxy and run our standard harness client. Option 1 gives higher fidelity to your runtime; option 2 is easier if you can't modify scripts.
[02:05] Marcus: We prefer minimal changes — option 2 would be ideal if it gives the same telemetry fidelity. Is there any difference in measured KV cache warmup or prefix caching if we go proxy vs shim?
[02:18] Elena: There can be. If the shim calls the Redwood SDK it will reuse the same client-side caching semantics (prefix cache, session-level KV). The proxy approach preserves traffic semantics but may hide some application-level caching behaviors. For a POC we recommend doing at least one run with the shim to capture warmup/steady-state differences.
[02:35] Leah: About warmup — our sessions are sticky, so simulating realistic session affinity matters for KV cache hits. Can your harness simulate sticky sessions?
[02:44] Elena: Yes, we have a session-affinity mode in the harness. We'll need your session key pattern and TTLs.
[02:51] Priya: We'll share that. Also, how do you instrument latency? We need p95 and p99 token latencies and end-to-end request latency including proxy handshakes.
[03:02] Samir: We capture both token-level latency (renderer-side) and end-to-end. The harness will emit p50/p95/p99 for token generation and request-level latencies, plus cpu/gpu utilization and network egress.
[03:15] Tom: What about streaming timeouts? Our proxy has an idle timeout of 60s. If a generation session stalls, the proxy sometimes tears connection and the client retries — that impacts your streaming results.
[03:26] Elena: We'll emulate that behavior in the test matrix. We'll also include scenario with jittered network latency to surface retry behavior.
[03:34] Marcus: Any specific footprint on the client side for the shim? We run Python-based microservices.
[03:40] Elena: Shim is a lightweight wrapper (~30-60 lines) that calls our SDK. It supports token refresh and attaches request metadata for tracing. No heavy deps.
[03:49] Priya: Ok. For acceptance criteria, here's what we propose: p95 end-to-end latency under 350ms for short prompts (≤128 tokens), p95 token latency under 200ms, max error rate under 1%, throughput sustaining 500 req/s for the steady window. Do those seem realistic?
[04:06] Samir: That's a bit aggressive but doable depending on model choice and quantization. If you pick a smaller open model we can meet those numbers on dedicated capacity. On hosted smaller instances the p95 might be higher. We'll capture model variants in the runbook.
[04:20] Leah: And tail latency? p99 under 800ms?
[04:24] Elena: That's reasonable as an initial target. We'll also include cold-start tail and warm steady-state numbers. 
[04:31] Tom: We also want cost per 1M tokens under $X — we'll fill in the number in the sheet.
[04:36] Samir: Ok we'll include a cost column.
[04:38] Marcus: Let's talk about telemetry. We need per-request trace IDs to correlate logs with our tracing system. Can the harness attach a trace header?
[04:45] Elena: Yes — we add a trace-id header and can push metrics to your Prometheus/Grafana endpoint or export to a CSV/BigQuery. What's your preferred sink?
[04:54] Marcus: Prometheus scrape would be easiest — we'll open a staging endpoint.
[04:58] Samir: Great. We'll configure the harness to push metrics and also dump raw events to the shared sheet for post-run analysis.
[05:06] Priya: About model variants — we want to test quantized 4-bit and float16; also prefer to evaluate a cheaper fallback model for high-traffic periods. Can the harness do automatic fallback testing?
[05:18] Elena: Yes, we can script a policy: baseline model then trigger fallback under saturated load to measure quality drop and latency improvement. We'll need questions sets to evaluate quality deltas.
[05:27] Leah: For quality we have 50 prompts we use for regression tests — we'll supply them. The harness supports BLEU-like scoring and human-review markers.
[05:36] Tom: About authentication, we use OAuth tokens with a short expiry (5m) and refresh flow. Will the harness handle token rotations?
[05:44] Elena: The shim handles token refresh; if you do proxy mode we'll need a token-refresh stub or to run behind your auth endpoint. Both ok.
[05:51] Samir: Quick note on network: if you're routing through a customer-managed VPC, we recommend doing an initial run with a small fleet to validate NAT/policy limits. Some customers hit ephemeral port exhaustion when the harness spins up many concurrent clients.
[06:06] Marcus: Good to know — we will check port ranges and NAT timeouts.
[06:10] Priya: Timeline — can we run the two-day benchmark next week?
[06:14] Samir: We have a slot on 2026-03-22 and 23 for pilot runs. We'll aim for the 22nd start and run through the 23rd morning to collect steady-state.
[06:23] Elena: I'll draft a test matrix: session affinity, streaming chunk size, idle timeouts, proxy burst behavior, model fallback triggers, and metric sinks. I'll post it to the runbook.
[06:34] Priya: Please include a scenario for mobile clients with high-latency networks, we want to see retry amplification effects.
[06:41] Elena: Will do.
[06:43] Tom: Are there any security documents you need to share before we run? We might need SOC2 attestation or a per-customer security addendum.
[06:52] Samir: We will send the security pack and SOC2 report. For the POC we can run under our standard terms but we can sign a limited SCA if needed.
[06:59] Leah: Also, for audit purposes we need request-level logs retained for 90 days in staging. Is that configurable?
[07:05] Elena: Yes we can keep logs for 90 days in the staging bucket and share access. We'll coordinate with your security contact.
[07:12] Priya: Ok, sounds good. I want to call out a risk: our proxy rewrites chunk boundaries for compression reasons, which can break client-side streaming parsers. If that's likely we'll need to test parsing/assembly on the client too.
[07:27] Elena: Noted — we can add a parsing-integrity check where the harness reassembles chunks and verifies completion semantics.
[07:34] Marcus: On failure modes, will the harness simulate partial failures mid-stream?
[07:39] Samir: Yes, failure injection is part of our test harness. We can kill streams, drop connections, and add latency spikes. We'll label the scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[07:49] Priya: Can you also capture retry amplification metrics? We saw amplification in our internal tests and want to quantify cost impact.
[07:57] Elena: We'll add a retry amplification calculation column in the output sheet: retries per original request and net token delta.
[08:05] Tom: Great. For deliverables, what will we get after the pilot?
[08:09] Samir: A run report: raw metrics, cost estimates, a short executive summary, and recommendations for tuning (batching, quantization, routing). We'll also flag any compatibility fixes for your client scripts.
[08:19] Priya: Perfect. Please include recommended guardrails for production rollouts.
[08:22] Elena: We'll add rollout suggestions: canary percentages, rate limit thresholds, and suggested fallback policies.
